prompt:
# Write one behaviour-tree node that ADJUSTS an existing navigator

You are writing a single node for the behaviour tree of a Unitree Go2 quadruped
navigating an indoor space it has no map of.

Below the node is an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy. The
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. You never
touch the policy, the gait, or the joints.

**You are not writing the navigator.** A navigator already exists, it already
drives, and it will keep driving whether or not your node does anything. Your
node sits above it and revises what it asked for.

Return **one Python module**, in one fenced ```python block, and nothing else
that looks like code. Everything you want to say in prose, say outside the
fence. What the module must contain is set out in "What to return" at the end.

## How the tree runs: a layered command pipeline

Every node in the tree ticks, **every step, in order**. Nothing short-circuits
anything.

    Layer[ ports, BASE, node_1, node_2, ... ]
             ^      ^      ^
             |      |      `- each may revise the fields it declared
             |      `-------- proposes a whole command, every tick
             `--------------- publishes a few facts from the sensors

The **base** is a general indoor navigator. It gets the robot most of the way
most of the time, it handles the awkward cases, and it never declines to act.
Each later node may then adjust individual fields of what the base proposed.

This is subsumption: a competent low layer, refined by narrow higher ones. Your
node is one of the higher ones.

**So the thing you are writing is small.** It does one thing to one part of the
command, under one condition, and the rest of the time it stays out of the way.

## The one hard rule: you declare which fields you may write

Your class declares `WRITES` — the Twist fields it is allowed to touch:

```python
WRITES = ("vx",)            # may bound or set forward speed, nothing else
WRITES = ("wz",)            # may steer, but may not change speed
WRITES = ("vx", "wz")       # both. Only if the mechanism genuinely needs both.
```

This is **enforced, not advisory.** Writing a field you did not declare raises
immediately and the node is rejected. Declare the smallest set your mechanism
actually needs — a node that declares all three is claiming to be a navigator,
and it will be judged as one.

Two ways to write, and they are the only two:

```python
ports.cap(vx=0.35)       # min(|pending|, 0.35), sign kept. Never speeds up.
ports.adjust(wz=0.8)     # replaces the field outright. Last writer wins.
```

Prefer `cap` whenever the mechanism is a limit, a bound, or a "no faster than"
— it composes with other caps in any order, which `adjust` does not.

And you can see what the base asked for:

```python
pending = ports.command          # a Command(vx, vy, wz). Never None when you
                                 # tick, because the base ticks before you.
if pending.vx > my_limit:
    ports.cap(vx=my_limit)
```

**Do not call `ports.drive(...)`.** That writes the whole command and is the
base's job; it raises for a node that narrowed `WRITES`.

## Declining is a first-class outcome, and it is free

Return `Status.FAILURE` from `precondition`, or simply write nothing in `tick`,
and the base's command passes through **byte-identical**. The robot behaves
exactly as if your node were not in the tree.

That matters more than it sounds. Your node's contribution is measured by adding
it to the tree and re-running the same worlds: it can only be credited for the
episodes it changes, and it is blamed for every episode it breaks. A node that
acts only when its trigger genuinely holds is a good node. A node that fires on
every tick has replaced the base rather than supported it, and it will be
measured as having done so.

## The node contract

A leaf is one of three kinds, and the kind is the class you subclass:

- **`Condition`** — answers one question about the world and publishes it as a
  port. Never touches the Twist.
- **`Action`** — the only kind that may touch the Twist. With a narrowed
  `WRITES` it is a *modifier*, which is what you are writing.
- **`Decorator`** — wraps exactly one child and governs whether the child runs.
  Never touches the Twist itself.

Your class declares, as class attributes:

| Attribute | What it is |
|---|---|
| `WRITES` | the Twist fields this node may write. See above. |
| `PORTS` | a tuple of `Port` — the typed interface between nodes. See below. |
| `PRECONDITION` | one sentence: when this node applies |
| `EFFECT` | one sentence: what this node changes |
| `TAGS` | a tuple of short strings, for retrieval |

and implements:

```python
def reset(self, scenario, rng):    # clear per-episode state. optional.
def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:   # default: always True
def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:         # Status.SUCCESS / FAILURE / RUNNING
```

**One precondition and one effect.** A node that needs two of either is two
nodes. This is not a style rule: contribution is measured by adding one node at
a time, and a node with two effects is attributable to neither.

**No coupling to a specific scenario.** Your node will be run on procedurally
generated worlds you have never seen. It may not name a room, a coordinate, a
doorway or a map. Anything it knows about the world it learns through `obs` at
tick time.

### Ports

Ports are how nodes pass information to each other. They are **not** a
blackboard: at tick time you are handed a `PortView` restricted to exactly the
ports you declared, and touching anything else raises immediately.

```python
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.IN)    # you read it:   value = ports["name"]
Port(name, PortType.X, Direction.OUT)   # you write it:  ports["name"] = value
```

The port vocabulary is **closed**. These seven types and no others:

| `PortType` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `POSE` | `(x, y, yaw)` — a belief about where the robot is, never ground truth |
| `BEARING` | radians, robot frame unless the port name says otherwise |
| `SPEED` | m/s, non-negative |
| `RANGES` | an array of beam returns, metres |
| `CONFIDENCE` | `[0, 1]` — how much to trust something |
| `FLAG` | a boolean fact about the episode |
| `REGION` | an area of the floor, `(x, y, radius)` |

Three ports are always published before your node ticks, so you may declare any
of them as inputs: `goal_known` (FLAG), `pose` (POSE), `ranges` (RANGES).
Anything else you declare as an input must be published by another node earlier
in the Layer, and if nothing does, the tree refuses to build.

Publish an OUT port when the quantity you computed is genuinely useful to
someone else — a limit, a bearing, a confidence. Do not publish your own
internal state.

### What to import

Exactly these, and nothing else.

```python
import math
import numpy as np

from core.observation import Command
from nodes.contract import (Action, Condition, Decorator, Direction, Port,
                            PortType, Status)
```

Import only what you use. You will usually not need `Command` at all: a modifier
revises fields, it does not construct commands.

### What your node can see

`tick` is handed an `Observation`, frozen, one per control step:

```python
obs.t                   # sim seconds since the episode started
obs.ranges              # np.ndarray, 181 beams, metres, inf where no return
obs.range_angles        # np.ndarray, beam bearings in the ROBOT frame, radians
obs.range_max           # 6.0 — what "as far as I can see" means
obs.pose_estimate       # (x, y, yaw) — the BELIEF about our pose, not the truth
obs.pose_error_estimate # scalar, metres — how wrong we think the belief is
obs.contact             # bool — are we touching something right now
obs.goal                # (x, y), or None meaning NOT DISCLOSED
```

Two of these are traps and both are deliberate:

- **`pose_estimate` is a belief.** On some scenarios a seeded random walk is
  added to it and it drifts away from the truth. Ground truth is never in
  `Observation`; the runner keeps it for scoring only.
- **`obs.goal` may be `None`**, meaning the goal exists and the episode is still
  scored against it, but this robot has not found it yet. It **latches**: once
  disclosed it stays disclosed. Your node runs on scenarios that withhold the
  goal and on scenarios that do not, so **handle `None` explicitly**. Do not
  assume a tuple.

The scan is 181 beams over a full circle, so `obs.ranges[0]` is not the front —
find the beam you want through `obs.range_angles`.

Speeds are saturated by the runner to `|vx|, |vy| <= 0.8 m/s` and
`|wz| <= 1.0 rad/s`. Asking for more is not an error; it is just clipped.

## The task family this node has to be useful for

Reach a goal whose position is known, in an indoor space with no map. Walls and furniture occlude; the route is not a straight line and the obstruction is often not visible until the robot is close to it.

## What to base the node on

A principle card has been written for this task. **Implement this principle and
nothing else.**

```yaml

node_name: SelectDynamicWindowVelocity

mechanism: Do not pick a direction and then a command; pick the command directly, by searching the two-dimensional space of velocity pairs (v, ω) that the body can actually reach in the next control interval. Each pair is read as a circular arc the robot would follow if it held that command, so obstacle checking is a circle-intersection test rather than a plan. The search space is pruned twice. First to the ADMISSIBLE set: Eq. (14), "Va = {(v, ω) | v ≤ sqrt(2 · dist(v,ω) · v̇_b) ∧ ω ≤ sqrt(2 · dist(v,ω) · ω̇_b)}", i.e. only commands from which braking at the maximum rate still stops the robot short of the nearest obstacle lying on that arc. Second to the DYNAMIC WINDOW, Eq. (15), "Vd = {(v, ω) | v ∈ [va - v̇·Δt, va + v̇·Δt] ∧ ω ∈ [ωa - ω̇·Δt, ωa + ω̇·Δt]}" — the commands reachable from the current one within one interval. Over what survives, Vr = Vs ∩ Va ∩ Vd (Eq. 16), maximise Eq. (13), "G(v, ω) = σ(α · heading(v,ω) + β · dist(v,ω) + γ · vel(v,ω))", each term normalised to [0,1] (Sec. 4.2, "Smoothing"), with α = 0.8, β = 0.1, γ = 0.1 (Sec. 5.4). The paper is explicit that all three terms are needed: "By solely maximizing the target heading the robot quickly would get stopped by the first obstacle that blocks its way, unable to move around it."

If the admissible set is empty — no command lets the robot translate and still stop — this leaf must FAIL rather than emit anything, and hand over to a recovery behaviour (the paper's separate "rotate away mode", Sec. 5.3, is a different card and is deliberately not included here). The paper's other Sec. 5.3 addition, the speed-dependent side clearance, is likewise excluded.

I resolve this by always commanding vy = 0 and searching only (vx, wz), which makes the paper's arc geometry (Eq. 10-12, radius v/ω) exactly valid — that restriction is mine, not the paper's. Vs is therefore vx ∈ [0, 0.8] m/s, wz ∈ [-1.0, 1.0] rad/s; reverse translation is not sampled (mine), because the frozen policy is not characterised backwards. ACCELERATIONS. The paper's dynamics come from motor torque limits; here the locomotion policy is frozen and exposes none, so I reinterpret v̇, ω̇ as a slew-rate limit on the issued Twist, preserving the paper's window-to-range ratio. RHINO: v̇·Δt = 0.5 · 0.25 = 0.125 m/s on a 0.9 m/s range (0.139), and ω̇·Δt = 60 deg/s² · 0.25 = 15 deg/s = 0.262 rad/s on a 1.571 rad/s range (0.167). Scaling to our limits gives Δv = 0.11 m/s and Δω = 0.175 rad/s per interval; with the paper's Δt = 0.25 s cycle that is v̇ = v̇_b = 0.45 m/s² and ω̇ = ω̇_b = 0.7 rad/s². The observation carries no velocity, so (va, ωa) in Eq. (15) is the Twist issued on the previous step (mine); on the first step after activation use (0, 0). GRID. Recompute every control step, emit only the first command (Sec. 4.1 justification (b),(c)). Sample 7 values of v across [max(0, va - 0.11), min(0.8, va + 0.11)] and 15 values of ω across [max(-1.0, ωa - 0.175), min(1.0, ωa + 0.175)] — resolution is mine, the paper only says "by discretization of the resulting search space". dist(v, ω) FROM LIDAR. The paper's obstacle line field from 24 sonar cones becomes the 181-beam scan directly: obstacle points p_i = (r_i cos θ_i, r_i sin θ_i) in the robot frame for every finite r_i ≤ 6.0.   baseline: reactive_avoid
  min_effect: 0.4
  cost_metric: time_to_goal
```

The fields mean what they say, and each one has a job:

- **mechanism** — what happens, and why it helps. This is the node body.
- **trigger** — when it applies. This is the precondition, and under the layered
  pipeline it is doing real work: outside the trigger your node must leave the
  base's command alone.
- **derivation** — how the principle becomes a rule for a Go2 with a 181-beam 2D
  scan. Where the derivation and your instincts disagree, follow the derivation:
  it is what the card is for.
- **prediction** — the falsifiable claim. **Restate it verbatim** in
  `PREDICTION`: the metric, the baseline and the minimum effect are the card's,
  not yours.
- **node_name** — what the leaf is called. Use it as the class name.

You are not told where this principle came from, and you do not need to know.
A card is a card: extracted from a paper, recalled from one, or devised from
nothing, it is implemented the same way and judged by the same harness.

If you believe a different mechanism would score better, that belief is not what
is being measured here — a node that quietly implements something else makes the
card untestable.

**If the principle genuinely cannot be expressed as an adjustment to an existing
navigator, say so in prose and write the closest honest version you can.** Some
mechanisms are whole navigators and this pipeline cannot represent them; that is
a finding about the corpus, and it is more useful than a node that pretends.

## How this node will be judged

Two steps, both automatic, neither of which you can talk round.

1. **Validity.** Your module is loaded, wired into
   `Layer[ports, BASE, your node]`, and ticked over a rollout. It has to build,
   its ports have to be satisfiable, and it must not raise. Writing a Twist
   field you did not declare fails here.
2. **Contribution.** The tree above is run over a suite of randomly generated
   indoor worlds and compared, on identical worlds, against the base alone. What
   is reported is how many worlds your node **fixed** (the base failed, the pair
   succeeded) and how many it **broke** (the reverse).

You do not write the worlds and you have never seen them. There is no
micro-world to build and no baseline to name — that is deliberate, because a
generator that writes both the mechanism and the world that judges it is
grading its own homework.

## Rules the candidate is checked against

Your module is rejected, automatically, if any of these is false. The rejection
is recorded with its reason; it is not a catastrophe, but it is a wasted node.

- It parses, and it imports **only** from this list:
  `math`, `numpy`, `core.observation`, `nodes.contract`, `harness.micro`.
  Nothing else — no `os`, no file access, no `core.scenario`, no `core.geometry`.
  Your node learns about the world through `obs`, and that restriction is what
  makes "no coupling to a specific scenario" true rather than promised.
- It defines **exactly one** `Condition`, `Action` or `Decorator` subclass.
- Every port type is one of the seven. `EFFECT` and `PRECONDITION` are non-empty.
- `WRITES` names only `vx`, `vy` and `wz`, and the node writes nothing outside
  it.

## What to return

One fenced ```python block. It contains exactly two things:

1. **One node class** — normally an `Action` with a narrowed `WRITES`.
2. **`PREDICTION`** — a module-level dict, the card's falsifiable claim:

   ```python
   PREDICTION = {
       "metric": "goal_reached",     # what gets better
       "baseline": "base",           # what it gets better than
       "min_effect": 0.5,            # by at least how much
       "cost_metric": "time_to_goal" # what it makes WORSE. Required, and honest.
   }
   ```

   `cost_metric` may be `""` only if you genuinely believe the mechanism costs
   nothing, and you should be suspicious of that belief.

**No `micro()`.** Do not write one; it is not read.

Put a short docstring on the class saying what mechanism it implements, which
Twist field it revises and why, and when it declines. Write it as you would
write code someone else has to maintain: comments where a choice is not obvious,
and no comments restating the line below them.

response.text:
Two honest caveats before the code.

**This card is a whole local navigator, not a modifier.** Dynamic-window selection picks `(v, ω)` jointly from scratch every tick; there is no way to express it as a bound on one field. The closest faithful form in this pipeline is an `Action` that `adjust`s both `vx` and `wz` — it overwrites the base rather than refining it, and it should be read (and measured) as a replacement local planner that hands control back to the base whenever its admissible set is empty, the goal is undisclosed, or the robot is in contact. I've kept the trigger tight for exactly that reason: outside it the base's bytes pass through untouched.

**I declared `vy` as well, and that needs justifying.** The derivation is explicit that the arc geometry of Eq. (10–12) is only valid because the command is restricted to `(v, ω)` with `vy = 0`; the admissibility proof in Eq. (14) is about stopping along *that arc*. If the base is strafing and I leave `vy` alone, every `dist(v,ω)` I compute is measuring the wrong curve, and the one guarantee the card buys — never entering a state you cannot brake out of — is void. So `vy` is zeroed, via `cap(vy=0.0)` rather than `adjust`, because zeroing lateral motion is a limit and composes as one. That makes three declared fields, which the brief warns will be judged as a navigator. It is a navigator; I would rather say so than narrow `WRITES` and ship a silently unsound admissibility test.

Everything else follows the derivation literally: the four slew numbers (Δv = 0.11, Δω = 0.175, v̇_b = 0.45, ω̇_b = 0.7), the 7×15 grid, `R_infl = 0.50`, α/β/γ = 0.8/0.1/0.1, the 3×3 box blur as σ, `(va, ωa)` taken as the previously *issued* Twist with `(0, 0)` on the first step after activation, and `dist = range_max` both for "no obstacle on the arc" and for `v = 0` candidates. Only the heading term reads `pose_estimate`, so pose drift degrades this into a collision-free wander rather than a crash. The one OUT port is the braking-admissible speed bound at the chosen command, which is genuinely a limit another node could cap against.

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from nodes.contract import Action, Direction, Port, PortType, Status


class SelectDynamicWindowVelocity(Action):
    """Dynamic-window velocity selection (Fox, Burgard & Thrun, Eq. 13-16).

    Instead of choosing a heading and then a speed, this node searches the
    two-dimensional space of velocity pairs (vx, wz) reachable within one
    control interval, reads each pair as the circular arc the body would
    follow if it held that command, and keeps only the pairs from which
    braking at the maximum rate still stops the robot short of the nearest
    obstacle on that arc.  Over the survivors it maximises a smoothed
    weighted sum of goal heading, clearance and speed.

    Revises vx and wz because the mechanism selects the pair jointly -- the
    admissibility test in Eq. (14) couples them through dist(v, w), so
    neither field can be chosen without the other.  Caps vy to zero because
    the arc geometry (and therefore the braking guarantee) is only valid for
    a command with no lateral component; that restriction is the derivation's
    resolution of the paper's non-holonomic synchro-drive onto a holonomic
    Twist.

    Declines -- leaving the base command byte-identical -- when the goal has
    not been disclosed, when the robot is already in contact, or when no
    candidate in the sampled window is admissible.  The last case is the
    paper's hand-off to a separate recovery behaviour ("rotate away mode",
    Sec. 5.3), which is a different card and is deliberately not implemented
    here.
    """

    WRITES = ("vx", "vy", "wz")
    PORTS = (Port("safe_speed_limit", PortType.SPEED, Direction.OUT),)
    PRECONDITION = (
        "The goal is disclosed and the robot is not currently in contact."
    )
    EFFECT = (
        "Replaces the commanded velocity with the highest-scoring pair in the "
        "admissible dynamic window, so that braking to a stop before the "
        "nearest obstacle on the committed arc always remains possible."
    )
    TAGS = ("dwa", "velocity-space", "admissible", "clearance", "local-planner")

    # Search space Vs.  Reverse translation is not sampled: the frozen
    # locomotion policy is not characterised backwards.
    V_MAX = 0.8
    W_MAX = 1.0

    # Slew limits per control interval, and the braking accelerations they
    # imply at the paper's dt = 0.25 s cycle.  Obtained by holding RHINO's
    # window-to-range ratios fixed against our own limits.
    DV = 0.11
    DW = 0.175
    DT = 0.25
    ACC_V = 0.45
    ACC_W = 0.7

    N_V = 7
    N_W = 15

    # Circumscribed Go2 radius ~0.40 m plus a 0.10 m margin.
    R_INFL = 0.50

    ALPHA = 0.8
    BETA = 0.1
    GAMMA = 0.1

    W_STRAIGHT = 1e-3
    V_STOPPED = 1e-6

    def reset(self, scenario, rng):
        self._prev_v = 0.0
        self._prev_w = 0.0
        self._active = False

    def precondition(self, obs, ports) -> bool:
        if getattr(obs, "goal", None) is None:
            return False
        if obs.contact:
            return False
        return True

    def tick(self, obs, ports) -> Status:
        if not getattr(self, "_active", False):
            # First step after activation: Eq. (15) is anchored at rest,
            # since the observation carries no measured body velocity.
            self._prev_v = 0.0
            self._prev_w = 0.0

        range_max = float(obs.range_max)
        px, py = self._obstacle_points(obs, range_max)

        v_grid = np.linspace(
            max(0.0, self._prev_v - self.DV),
            min(self.V_MAX, self._prev_v + self.DV),
            self.N_V,
        )
        w_grid = np.linspace(
            max(-self.W_MAX, self._prev_w - self.DW),
            min(self.W_MAX, self._prev_w + self.DW),
            self.N_W,
        )

        scores = np.zeros((self.N_V, self.N_W), dtype=float)
        admissible = np.zeros((self.N_V, self.N_W), dtype=bool)
        dists = np.zeros((self.N_V, self.N_W), dtype=float)

        goal = obs.goal
        pose = obs.pose_estimate

        for i, v in enumerate(v_grid):
            for j, w in enumerate(w_grid):
                dist = self._arc_distance(v, w, px, py, range_max)
                dists[i, j] = dist

                # Eq. (14): keep only commands we can still brake out of.
                if v > math.sqrt(2.0 * dist * self.ACC_V):
                    continue
                if abs(w) > math.sqrt(2.0 * dist * self.ACC_W):
                    continue
                admissible[i, j] = True

                heading = self._heading_term(v, w, pose, goal)
                clearance = dist / range_max
                # A stationary candidate scores no speed reward, so pure
                # rotation only wins when nothing that translates survives.
                speed = 0.0 if v <= self.V_STOPPED else v / self.V_MAX
                scores[i, j] = (
                    self.ALPHA * heading
                    + self.BETA * clearance
                    + self.GAMMA * speed
                )

        if not admissible.any():
            # No command is recoverable: hand back to the base, and re-anchor
            # the window at rest for whenever we next activate.
            self._active = False
            return Status.FAILURE

        smoothed = self._smooth(scores, admissible)
        smoothed = np.where(admissible, smoothed, -np.inf)
        i, j = np.unravel_index(int(np.argmax(smoothed)), smoothed.shape)

        best_v = float(v_grid[i])
        best_w = float(w_grid[j])

        # Only the first command of the plan is emitted; the whole search is
        # redone next step against a fresh scan.
        ports.adjust(vx=best_v, wz=best_w)
        ports.cap(vy=0.0)

        ports["safe_speed_limit"] = float(
            np.clip(math.sqrt(2.0 * dists[i, j] * self.ACC_V), 0.0, self.V_MAX)
        )

        self._prev_v = best_v
        self._prev_w = best_w
        self._active = True
        return Status.SUCCESS

    def _obstacle_points(self, obs, range_max):
        """Scan returns as points in the robot frame, as the paper's obstacle
        line field but taken straight off the 181 beams."""
        ranges = np.asarray(obs.ranges, dtype=float)
        angles = np.asarray(obs.range_angles, dtype=float)
        valid = np.isfinite(ranges) & (ranges > 0.0) & (ranges <= range_max)
        if not valid.any():
            empty = np.empty(0, dtype=float)
            return empty, empty
        r = ranges[valid]
        a = angles[valid]
        return r * np.cos(a), r * np.sin(a)

    def _arc_distance(self, v, w, px, py, range_max):
        """Distance along the arc (v, w) to the first inflated obstacle,
        saturated at range_max, which is also the paper's "large constant"
        for an arc with nothing on it."""
        if px.size == 0:
            return range_max
        if v <= self.V_STOPPED:
            return range_max

        if abs(w) < self.W_STRAIGHT:
            ahead = (np.abs(py) <= self.R_INFL) & (px > 0.0)
            if not ahead.any():
                return range_max
            return float(np.clip(px[ahead].min() - self.R_INFL, 0.0, range_max))

        radius = v / w
        cy = radius
        d = np.hypot(px, py - cy)
        hit = np.abs(d - abs(radius)) <= self.R_INFL
        if not hit.any():
            return range_max

        # Sweep angle from the robot's own bearing about the arc centre,
        # measured in the direction of travel; the paper's "gamma * r",
        # renamed phi here to keep gamma for the objective weight.
        a0 = math.atan2(-radius, 0.0)
        ap = np.arctan2(py[hit] - cy, px[hit])
        phi = np.mod(math.copysign(1.0, w) * (ap - a0), 2.0 * math.pi)
        return float(min(abs(radius) * float(phi.min()), range_max))

    def _heading_term(self, v, w, pose, goal):
        """1 - |theta|/pi, with theta the goal bearing from the pose reached
        after one interval on this arc plus the braking tail."""
        x, y, yaw = float(pose[0]), float(pose[1]), float(pose[2])

        if abs(w) < self.W_STRAIGHT:
            x += v * self.DT * math.cos(yaw)
            y += v * self.DT * math.sin(yaw)
        else:
            radius = v / w
            yaw_next = yaw + w * self.DT
            x += radius * (math.sin(yaw_next) - math.sin(yaw))
            y += radius * (math.cos(yaw) - math.cos(yaw_next))
            yaw = yaw_next

        yaw += math.copysign(w * w / (2.0 * self.ACC_W), w)
        brake_travel = v * v / (2.0 * self.ACC_V)
        x += brake_travel * math.cos(yaw)
        y += brake_travel * math.sin(yaw)

        theta = self._wrap(math.atan2(float(goal[1]) - y, float(goal[0]) - x) - yaw)
        return 1.0 - abs(theta) / math.pi

    def _smooth(self, scores, admissible):
        """sigma from Eq. (13), as a 3x3 box blur that averages only over
        admissible neighbours so inadmissible cells cannot drag a score down."""
        weights = admissible.astype(float)
        padded_s = np.pad(scores * weights, 1, mode="constant")
        padded_w = np.pad(weights, 1, mode="constant")
        rows, cols = scores.shape

        num = np.zeros_like(scores)
        den = np.zeros_like(scores)
        for dy in range(3):
            for dx in range(3):
                num += padded_s[dy:dy + rows, dx:dx + cols]
                den += padded_w[dy:dy + rows, dx:dx + cols]

        return np.where(den > 0.0, num / np.maximum(den, 1e-9), scores)

    @staticmethod
    def _wrap(angle):
        return (angle + math.pi) % (2.0 * math.pi) - math.pi


PREDICTION = {
    "metric": "collisions",
    "baseline": "reactive_avoid",
    "min_effect": 0.4,
    "cost_metric": "time_to_goal",
}
```

On the cost metric: `time_to_goal` is the right one and it is not a formality. The admissibility test is what makes the robot decelerate into tight passages, so on exactly the episodes where it prevents a collision it also spends longer getting through — that is the same effect measured twice, once as a benefit and once as a cost.
